cf.title: Doc: clarify pg_locks descriptions of classid/objid/objsubid

input.subject: Doc: clarify pg_locks descriptions of classid/objid/objsubid

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The patch corrects column descriptions in system-views.sgml that contradict the per-lock-type prose under the same table, and it changes no behavior. A committer agreed with the direction in message #2 and registered as committer. Confidence is medium because the v2 wording is not shown.

brief.title: Doc: fix pg_locks descriptions of classid, objid and objsubid
brief.problem: The pg_locks docs say classid, objid and objsubid are null when the lock target is not a general database object. pg_lock_status() also fills these columns for advisory, speculative insertion and apply transaction locks, so the column table contradicts the prose below it. Users reading pg_locks get a wrong description.
brief.proposed_design: Each column description is scoped to the general database object case and points to the per-lock-type prose below, without listing the other lock types. The prose for apply transaction locks now says objid shows the subscription OID. In v2, Fujii Masao also scoped the "references" notes, updated the introductory paragraph and linked the subscription OID to pg_subscription.oid.
user_visible_surface: Changed documentation of pg_locks columns classid, objid and objsubid in system-views.sgml.
New documented meaning of pg_locks.objid for apply transaction locks: the subscription OID.
author_claims: The current column descriptions are false for advisory, speculative insertion and apply transaction locks.
Not listing the non-object lock types in the column descriptions keeps them from drifting as new lock types are added.
The change is documentation only; no behavior changes.
brief.thread_state: Fujii Masao agreed with the direction, posted v2 with extra edits and registered himself as committer. The author has not replied to v2.
unclear: Only the v1 hunk is shown, so reviewers cannot see the exact v2 wording.
The thread does not say whether the fix should be back-patched to supported branches.
The thread does not say whether any lock type still leaves these columns null, which the new text no longer mentions.

committability.liability: The wording of three column descriptions and one paragraph in system-views.sgml; the cost is a later doc correction if a lock type is described wrongly.

precedents_retrieved.title: Document AccessExclusive lock behaviour on standbys
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds text to the table-level locks section of the explicit locking documentation. It states that an AccessExclusive lock on the primary is written to WAL and replayed on standbys, so the table is also locked there, and for how long.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The thread has only the author's first message, with no reply from a reviewer, and the entry was later withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: Lockable views
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets LOCK TABLE work on automatically updatable views without INSTEAD OF rules or triggers. Locking such a view also locks its base relation, recursively through nested views.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas questioned the core behavior and expected LOCK TABLE on a view to lock only the view, pointing to earlier discussion. Michael Paquier agreed and returned the patch because the author had not replied to that objection for one month.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I would have expected LOCK TABLE v to lock the view and nothing else.

precedents_retrieved.title: Moving relation extension locks out of heavyweight lock manager
precedents_retrieved.summary: Move relation extension locks out of the heavyweight lock manager into a separate lightweight mechanism in shared memory, because these locks need neither multiple lock modes nor deadlock detection. The first draft used a shared hash table of LWLocks; later versions used a fixed-size array of lock entries (N_RELEXTLOCK_ENTS) indexed by a hash of the relation, so a backend can find and reuse a lock's address without a mapping lock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks showed regressions of up to 25% when different relations hashed to the same lock entry. Andres Freund was not convinced that such false collisions would be rare, citing partitioning and the birthday paradox, and doubted that a larger array would fix it. Robert Haas argued that removing collisions would require a mapping lock and extra atomic operations on every extension, and the question was not resolved. The thread then went quiet, and Michael Paquier returned the entry because it seemed hard to reach a committable state for v11.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Also, birthday paradoxon and all that make collisions not that unlikely. And you really don't need a 16 way conflict to feel pain, you'll imo feel it earlier.

precedents_retrieved.title: Moving relation extension locks out of heavyweight lock manager
precedents_retrieved.summary: Move relation extension locks out of the heavyweight lock manager into a shared hash table of LWLock-like entries that are looked up per relation. The patch targeted lower overhead and future parallel utility commands such as parallel vacuum.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch in November 2018 after it no longer applied and needed a rebase. His parallel vacuum work had narrowed to parallel index vacuum, which does not need this change. Earlier in the thread, reviewers raised interruptibility and deadlock concerns, and a March 2018 commitfest closed the entry for lack of activity. The visible messages do not show these concerns as the deciding reason.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Therefore, I want to withdraw this patch and to reactivate when we need this enhancement.

precedents_retrieved.title: Surround CheckRelation[Oid]LockedByMe() with USE_ASSERT_CHECKING
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch declares and defines CheckRelationLockedByMe() and CheckRelationOidLockedByMe() only under USE_ASSERT_CHECKING, because core uses them only in assertions. This would drop them from non-assert builds.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Out-of-core code may call these functions for runtime checks in non-assert builds. An extension built with assertions enabled can also run against a core server built without them, the same reason ExceptionalCondition() is not ifdef'd away. The author agreed and withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Also, I believe it's possible for an extension that's been
built with assertions enabled to be used with a core server that
wasn't.  This is why, for example, ExceptionalCondition() is not
ifdef'd away in a non-assert build.

precedents_retrieved.title: group locking
precedents_retrieved.summary: Robert Haas proposed a heavyweight-lock concept of "locking groups" for parallelism: a user backend and its worker backends would form a group whose lock requests never conflict with each other, with changes to lock acquisition, wait-queue handling and the deadlock detector so that no group member waits behind an unrelated process. The posted patch was an incomplete draft (LockAcquireExtended() and ProcSleep() modified, ProcWakeup() and the deadlock detector not) meant to get feedback on the design.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the leader could hold the locks for its workers, and that the proposal added too much complexity, with bugs and performance costs, to the lock manager. Andres Freund objected that letting group members hold self-exclusive locks at the same time removes guarantees that existing code relies on, citing transaction abort (smgrDoPendingDeletes) and relcache invalidation. Robert Haas then dropped the original design because it would put too much coordination burden on the workers, and moved to granting the leader's existing locks to workers at the start of a parallel operation. The visible thread ends without agreement on that alternative or a revised patch, and the closing decision is not shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Based on your arguments and those of others, I have long-since abandoned the original proposal of having locks within a group never conflict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add pg_ownerships and pg_privileges system views
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds two system views, pg_privileges (first named pg_permissions) and pg_ownerships, that list privileges and ownerships across all catalogs, so a user can query everything granted to or owned by one role. Later versions build pg_privileges on pg_shdepend and a pg_get_acl() function, avoiding a long UNION ALL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last message is a rebase in October 2024 onto the committed three-argument pg_get_acl(), and no later reply or objection is shown before the entry was withdrawn in January 2025.

precedents_retrieved.title: Restore lock level to update statusFlags
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Restore lock level to update statusFlags
Reverted commit(s): Relax lock level for setting PGPROC->statusFlags
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Reverts 27838981be9d (some comments are kept).  Per discussion, it does
not seem safe to relax the lock level used for this; in order for it to
be safe, there would have to be memory barriers between the point we set
the flag and the point we set the trasaction Xid, which perhaps would
not be so bad; but there would also have to be barriers at the readers'
side, which from a performance perspective might be bad.

Now maybe this analysis is wrong and it *is* safe for some reason, but
proof of that is not trivial.

precedents_retrieved.title: transaction statistics of logical replication subscription
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread first proposed counting failed transactions and their sizes in pg_stat_replication_slots, so that users could tell successful logical decoding from repeated failed attempts. By the last version, the patch instead added apply_commit_count and apply_rollback_count columns to pg_stat_subscription_stats.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila noted that pg_stat_database already shows committed and rolled-back transactions per database, so the new counters largely duplicate it, and he asked whether anyone saw value in them. Masahiko Sawada agreed that commit and rollback counts without transaction sizes no longer meet the original goal and have no concrete use case. The author then marked the entry Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I’m concerned that adding only apply_commit_count
and apply_rollback_count ends up adding the duplicate statistics with
no concrete use cases.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the precedent search returned no earlier attempt at this idea, and the thread does not mention one. This is a docs-only fix that a committer has taken on, so a prior-attempts objection has nothing to rest on.

This is a documentation-only change to the pg_locks column descriptions. It changes no syntax, GUC, catalog, dump output, psql behaviour or client-visible result, so nothing on the standards and compatibility side breaks for existing users. The v1 text drops the remark that these columns are null for relation, page, tuple and transaction ID locks; reviewers of the v2 wording may want to check that the per-lock-type prose still covers those cases.

The patch changes only doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml. It adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, protocol or ABI change, so it creates no persistent or cross-node state. The new note that objid shows the subscription OID for apply transaction locks describes what pg_lock_status() already reports, as message #1 states.

The patch only changes the pg_locks column descriptions in system-views.sgml. It does not change who can read pg_locks or what pg_lock_status() returns. Documenting that objid shows the subscription OID for apply transaction locks describes data the view already exposes to anyone who can query it, so there is no privilege or exposure aspect.

This patch changes documentation only. It fixes column descriptions that contradict the prose under the same table, and it adds no hot-path cost, API, GUC or dependency. Not listing the non-object lock types lowers future drift, and a committer who knows the area has taken the patch on. Maintenance and fit give no ground to reject it. Back-patching was not discussed, and the v2 wording is not shown.
